titel: Blueprint Medicines: Chasing Gleevec to a $9B Allergy Drug

faehigkeiten.grund: Dynamik weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen: keine Merkmale gefunden, aber eine unveraenderte Wiederholungsprobe beweist nichts

einzeiler: How Blueprint Medicines built a $9B allergy drug empire from cancer research.
kurzfassung: Blueprint Medicines was founded by Third Rock Ventures to create a revolutionary kinase-inhibitor platform modeled after Gleevec. Despite facing severe financial near-death and clinical failures in oncology, the company unexpectedly discovered its true blockbuster opportunity in mastocytosis. Ultimately, this precision-cancer pioneer transformed into a specialized immunology player, culminating in a $9 billion acquisition by Sanofi.
stichpunkte: Third Rock Ventures founded Blueprint Medicines in 2011 to build a proprietary kinase inhibitor platform.
The company invested heavily in prescreening a massive chemical library against all human kinases.
Early fundraising was an extreme struggle, nearly leading to insolvency before a 2014 bridge round and 2015 IPO.
Avapritinib was discovered by hybridizing literature scaffolds and platform molecules to target mutant KIT.
Initial clinical strategies focused heavily on targeted oncology indications like GIST and RET-driven lung cancer.
Clinical trials revealed unexpected, highly potent efficacy against mastocytosis, shifting the company toward immunology.
Blueprint had to build the diagnostic and awareness ecosystem for systemic mastocytosis from scratch.
A massive $775 million partnership with Roche helped fund early commercialization before Roche returned the RET program.
Avapritinib achieved blockbuster status in indolent systemic mastocytosis due to chronic, multi-year patient dosing.
Sanofi acquired Blueprint Medicines for approximately $9 billion in cash to help combat impending patent cliffs.

clips.hook: A ludicrous amount of money spent on a prescreening bet that paid off big time.
clips.text: The company invested ten million dollars early on to screen every single kinase against a proprietary inhibitor library, a massive upfront gamble that ultimately generated two approved drugs across four indications within a decade.

clips.hook: Down to $100,000 in cash and on absolute vapor before a rescue check.
clips.text: The startup came dangerously close to missing its payroll due to running out of capital, surviving only because a small syndicate scraped together a bridge round when cash reserves dwindled to a nominal amount.

clips.hook: A tiny 30 milligram starting dose triggered unexpected biological effects.
clips.text: During early dose-escalation studies for an aggressive rare disease, researchers noticed that even at the absolute lowest tested dose, the molecule was already actively suppressing disease markers with minimal side effects.

beschreibung:
Blueprint Medicines was built to find the next Gleevec-style cancer drug. It ended up pivoting to allergic disease instead, and selling to Sanofi for $9B. This is the platform, the pivot, and who got paid.

Blueprint Medicines set out to be the natural sequel to Gleevec: a company founded by two of the scientists behind that landmark cancer drug, built to order by Third Rock Ventures' "venture creation" model, with a proprietary kinase-inhibitor library designed to drug the 517 other broken molecular switches Gleevec couldn't touch.
A decade later, Sanofi paid roughly $9 billion for the company... just not for a cancer drug. Blueprint's blockbuster asset, avapritinib (AYVAKIT), found its real market almost by accident: indolent systemic mastocytosis, a debilitating, often-undiagnosed mast-cell disease that took patients years to get diagnosed and had no approved treatment.

In this episode, we trace two threads at once: the science of designing truly selective kinase inhibitors, and the venture capital philosophy -- company creation, not just company funding -- that built Blueprint from a whiteboard sketch into a platform biotech. We cover the near-death Series B, the accidental discovery that opened up mastocytosis, the GAVRETO partnership that fell apart against a faster competitor, the Sanofi negotiation (CVRs and all), and the wide gap between what the venture firm and hired executives made versus what the founding scientists -- like Gleevec's co-inventor Nick Lydon -- walked away with. We end covering the efforts of Blueprint diaspora to create a new model of seed investing: Curie Bio.
